text.title: Mistake Memory Worked Examples
text.summary: Three worked artefacts for Mistake Memory: a MIS-NNN entry with a three-level Five Whys chain, the pre-task warning injection command, and a CI prevention rule generated from a recurring mistake.

example.title: MIS-007 with three levels of why and a concrete prevention
example.code:
## MIS-007: Database Migration — Missing Row Count Check
**Severity:** High **What happened:** Migration timed out after 30 min on production (2.8M rows). **Root cause:** 1. Why did migration time out? Transaction locked the entire table. 2. Why was it a single transaction? ALTER TABLE applied to all rows at once. 3. Why not batched? Row count not checked before choosing migration strategy. **Prevention:** Before any migration, run `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM <table>`. If >100k rows, use batched approach (PAT-002).
example.note: Three levels of why, specific numbers, concrete prevention with a reference to a known pattern.

example.title: Keyword-based warning injection before a migration task
example.code: # Load warnings before executing TASK-042 (database migration) ./inject-warnings.sh "database migration schema" | prepend-to-task TASK-042
example.note: Keywords match entries by domain, not by full-text similarity. Semantic matching is unreliable in prompts.

example.title: Prevention rule generated from a recurring destructive-migration mistake
example.code: # Prevention rule for destructive migrations (source: MIS-010) id: PREV_010 trigger: type: code_pattern pattern: "DROP (TABLE|COLUMN)" file_types: ["*.sql", "migrations/*"] action: type: block message: "Destructive migration detected. Take backup first. See MIS-010."
example.note: Applies r-recurrence-ci-rule: a file pattern plus code pattern detector that blocks, citing the MIS entry it was generated from.
